groups.title: Self-Improving Software Factories: The New Open Source Model

frames.alt: Title slide for Zach Lloyd’s talk at AI Engineer World’s Fair 2026.
frames.text:
Self-Improving Software Factories: The New Open Source Model

Zach Lloyd — Warp
AI Engineer World’s Fair 2026

warp

annotation.text: Zach Lloyd introduces his view of how development is changing through self-improving software factories and a new open source model.

frames.alt: Zach Lloyd’s engineering background and a portrait.
frames.text:
Zach Lloyd

• Principal engineer at Google, lead on GDocs
• 20 years of engineering
• Founder of Warp

annotation.text: Warp founder Zach Lloyd led engineering on Google Docs and has over 20 years of experience. He says he still ships frequently despite writing no code in the last six months.

frames.alt: Warp overview with open-source and developer statistics alongside a product screenshot.
frames.text:

• Open Source ADE
• 62K stars
• 800k+ active devs
• From the terminal to the cloud

annotation.text: Warp began as a terminal and now combines it with agents. Its screenshot places sessions, a terminal, and a code editor side by side; Lloyd says Warp is increasingly focused on automating development.

frames.alt: Thesis: software engineering will become factory engineering.
frames.text:
Thesis:

Software engineering will become factory engineering.

4

annotation.text: Lloyd predicts that software engineers will build and manage software factories, where agents and humans share work across development.

frames.alt: A timeline from chat and AI autocomplete through interactive agents to automated agents, with interactive agents marked as today.
frames.text:
The evolution of agentic development

Chat
AI Autocomplete
Interactive Agents
TODAY
Automated Agents

6

annotation.text: Lloyd places today at interactive agents, where developers direct tools from their computers. He expects a shift toward automation over the next six months to a year, though the pace is uncertain.

frames.alt: Audience question: How many of you are building with agents?
frames.text:
How many of you are
building with agents?

7

annotation.text: Lloyd asks for a show of hands and says 100% of the audience is building with agents.

frames.alt: Slide asks how many attendees are running multiple agents simultaneously.
frames.text:
How many of you are
running multiple agents
simultaneously?

8

annotation.text: Lloyd asks who typically builds with multiple agents at once; almost everyone raises a hand.

frames.alt: Slide asks how many attendees are running agents in the cloud.
frames.text:
How many of you are
running agents in the cloud?

9

annotation.text: Lloyd asks for a show of hands and estimates that less than half the audience is running agents in the cloud, though the number is significant.

frames.alt: Slide asks about automating the software lifecycle and lists triage, spec, implement, review, and ship.
frames.text:
How many of you are automating the whole software lifecycle?

Triage → Spec → Implement → Review → Ship

10

annotation.text: Lloyd asks who has automated the lifecycle from triage through shipping; some attendees raise their hands.

frames.alt: Circular software lifecycle diagram with triage, spec, implementation, verification, shipping, and monitoring, plus human review points.

11

annotation.text: Lloyd envisions agents triaging, implementing and verifying in a continuous loop, with humans reviewing specs, code and the product before shipping and monitoring.

frames.alt: Black slide asks, “What about Open Source?”
frames.text: What about Open Source?

annotation.text: Lloyd turns to open source, saying one reason Warp open sourced was to build a public factory.

annotation.text: Warp’s public factory dashboard tracks issues by workflow state and lists top contributors. Lloyd calls it a working but imperfect proto-factory.

frames.alt: Slide asks, “Why Open Source?”
frames.text:
Why Open Source?

15

annotation.text: Warp open sourced in part to build a public factory for software development.

frames.alt: A cost-versus-time graph shows a declining curve.
frames.text:
Cost to build:

Y-axis: COST
X-axis: TIME

16

annotation.text: Lloyd argues that software is becoming much cheaper to build. The curve falls steeply at first, then levels off over time.

frames.alt: A slide titled “Time to clone” shows the Same.dev website.
frames.text:
Time to clone:

17

annotation.text: Lloyd argues that cheaper development makes software trivial to clone, making it harder for software businesses to capture value. The slide shows Same.dev’s AI website builder.

frames.alt: The slide asks how to build a software business when it is free to build software.
frames.text:
How do you build a software business when it’s free to build software?

18

annotation.text: Lloyd asks how software businesses can capture value when competitors can easily clone their products.

frames.alt: A black slide says, “Tip 1: Patent your code.” The speaker identifies it as a joke.
frames.text: Tip 1: Patent your code.

annotation.text: After noting that competitors can easily clone software, Lloyd jokes about patenting code and explicitly tells the audience not to do it.

groups.title: You need a great product, but it is not enough

frames.alt: A slide says, “You need a great product...”
frames.text:
You need a great product...

20

frames.alt: A great product is necessary, but not enough.
frames.text:
You need a great product...
but a great product is not enough.

21

annotation.text: As software becomes easier to clone, Lloyd argues that a great product is essential but unlikely on its own to build a successful software business.

frames.alt: Distribution, ecosystem, community, brand, data and capital are listed as advantages beyond the product.
frames.text:
You need an advantage beyond the product.

Distribution → Ecosystem → Community →
Brand → Data → Capital

22

annotation.text: Lloyd names distribution, ecosystem, community, brand, data and capital as potential advantages beyond a great product.

frames.alt: Startups can still break through.
frames.text:
But startups can
still break through.

24

annotation.text: Lloyd recommends building in the open to help startups build an ecosystem. Warp made that shift after five years of closed development.

frames.alt: White text on black asks whether open source is a pain.
frames.text: But isn’t open source a pain?

annotation.text: Lloyd says building in the open can grow an ecosystem and community, while traditional burdens such as noisy issues and code review can now be managed.

annotation.text: Mock alerts illustrate the competing demands of open-source maintenance: failed releases, repeated tasks, review requests, rising errors, and urgent messages.

frames.alt: Four challenges: noisy issues, sloppy pull requests, code review, and verifying changes.
frames.text:
Noisy issues
Sloppy PRs
Code review hell
Verifying changes

31

annotation.text: Warp built a software factory of automations to manage its open-source project, addressing noisy issues, sloppy PRs, code review, and the work of verifying changes.
